paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Blackman refers to a manhunt in Schley County, Georgia, in June 1888, after Blackman, a Black man under sentence of death for the murder of Stonewall Tondee, escaped from the jail at Americus. A Macon dispatch printed in Richmond said large bodies of men had organized to hunt him and predicted a lynching if bloodhounds found him. No lynching followed: a Stewart County deputy sheriff captured Blackman in mid-June, and a court resentenced him to hang that fall.

Blackman had been convicted of shooting Tondee at night at the back door of the Ellaville store where, by differing accounts, Tondee was the merchant or a clerk. He was convicted three times, the state supreme court granting new trials twice before affirming the third judgment shortly before his escape. Schley County had lodged him in the Sumter County jail at Americus "for safe keeping."

On the night of Wednesday, June 6, Blackman left the Americus jail with a key that, according to the Savannah Morning News, a confederate had given him. The news caused "great excitement" and anger at jail officials who had let visitors see the prisoner without a guard, and the county commissioners offered a $250 reward. From Ellaville, a correspondent of the Atlanta Constitution wrote that residents denounced the Sumter jailer, some suggesting his complicity, and feared Blackman would "return and kill others here."

A Macon dispatch of June 10, carried by the Richmond Daily Times under the headline "Pursued by Bloodhounds," went further. It said Blackman was believed to be back in Schley County, where "large bodies of men have organized to run him down," and that there would be a lynching "if the bloodhoods do their duty." The same dispatch reported an open suspicion that some white man had prompted the killing of Tondee and was shielding Blackman from punishment. The Georgia reports of the escape and capture mention no organized crowd or lynching threat.

Deputy Sheriff Holder of Stewart County and his assistant Kendrick, described as "a trusty negro," caught Blackman on a Friday morning at Banks's landing as he was about to cross the Chattahoochee River. According to the Weekly Constitution, he "fought like a tiger," carried a pencil-marked map of a route to Mississippi, and was put in the dungeon of the Americus jail in heavy irons.

Holly Eubanks (printed "Embanks"), a Black man, was jailed at Americus on a charge of aiding the escape and released on $500 bond in July. Judge Fort declined to call a special term, so Blackman remained in the Americus jail until the September term of the Schley superior court. At Ellaville on a Wednesday in late September, Fort sentenced him to hang on October 19, after which the sheriff and guards took him back to Americus by train. On October 6 Governor Gordon respited him for sixty days so that a motion for a new trial could be made, and no later report of the case was found.

The surviving coverage comes from white newspapers, chiefly the Savannah Morning News and the Atlanta Constitution. Georgia papers called Blackman a "black fiend" and "fiend incarnate," likened his freedom to "a lion loose in our midst," and aimed their anger mainly at the jailer. Only the Macon dispatch in the Richmond paper presented the manhunt as a likely lynching, stating the prospect without criticism.

Later items treated the resentencing as the end of a long and costly case, the Constitution remarking that when he was "disposed of the county will breathe a breath of relief." A short paragraph on the sentence ran outside Georgia, including in the West Tennessee Star on October 5.

The Macon dispatch dated the Tondee killing to Christmas Eve three years earlier, while the Atlanta Constitution placed it in September 1885. The Weekly Constitution said Blackman was captured on a Friday morning but also that Holder reached Americus with him on Thursday.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Blackman
bases: The only mob-violence element is a Macon dispatch forecasting a lynching by organized men hunting the escaped prisoner (A2); he was recaptured by a deputy sheriff and returned to court custody (A5, A9).

No one was killed: Blackman was captured alive by a Stewart County deputy, jailed and resentenced by Judge Fort (A5, A9, A12). The Macon dispatch reported 'large bodies of men' hunting him and predicted a lynching, which is at most a threatened lynching (A2).

The escape, recapture and resentencing are corroborated across Georgia papers (A1, A3, A4, A5, A9, A10), but the organized pursuit and the prospect of a lynching appear only in the Macon dispatch printed in Richmond (A2).

accounts.label: Macon dispatch
accounts.gist: Blackman escaped with a false key from confederates; large bodies of men organized in Schley County to run him down, and a lynching would follow if the bloodhounds succeeded; suspicion that a white man prompted the Tondee killing.

accounts.label: Ellaville correspondent
accounts.gist: Residents cursed the Sumter jailer, some suggesting complicity, and feared Blackman would return to kill; 'We can do nothing' except curse those responsible.

accounts.label: Capture report
accounts.gist: Deputy Sheriff Holder and Kendrick caught Blackman crossing the Chattahoochee after a struggle; he was jailed in irons at Americus.

framing.detail: Macon dispatch headlined 'Pursued by Bloodhounds' states the prospect of a lynching matter-of-factly, without condemnation.
Georgia papers called Blackman a 'black fiend' and 'fiend incarnate' while aiming their anger at the jailer and calling for court punishment.
Later items report the resentencing and respite as court news, the Constitution noting the case's cost to Schley County.

conflicts.note: No account is clearly better; the Constitution gives the only specific month and year.
